How work gets planned, built and handed over

Kompass Skills

Kompass Skills plan a project properly, then build it in sequences of work units that run back to back without pausing. Every unit and every sequence ends with a written hand-over saved with the code, so the next agent picks up from the record and never from a session's memory.

How it fits together planunitsrunbuildfind Who does whatSafety

How it fits together

Plan once, then build sequence after sequence. Each sequence ends with a written hand-over and your walkthrough, and the next one starts from that record.

  1. PlanBrief, module map, architecture, UI mockups you click through, decisions. One approval.kompass-plan
  2. Write unitsOne-page briefs grouped into sequences, each ending at a point you can walk through.kompass-units
  3. Build a sequenceUnits built back to back, each in a fresh session with kompass-build.kompass-run
  4. Sequence hand-overWhat was achieved, what is parked, and walkthrough steps for you.kompass-run
  5. Your walkthroughYou try it; your words and any problems are recorded. Problems become the next sequence's first units.kompass-run
  6. Next sequenceStarts from the hand-over and your recorded walkthrough.kompass-run

The skills

Each skill is a short instruction file an agent follows. Questions in coral are open: they are what we decide next.

kompass-plan

104 lines

Plans a project or phase with you, before any code is written.

Use when: Start of a project or phase; re-planning; reviewing the plan.

Reads

  • Your brief and answers
  • The existing code, for a project already under way
  • The project's design tokens, for mockups

Leaves behind

  • Brief and approval record
  • Module map: purpose, front door, owned files, rules with their tests
  • Architecture with diagrams of each key journey
  • Interactive mockups for each UI decision
  • Decision records
  • Sequences: where each walkthrough falls
  • The planning page

Stops for you

  • Only for your answers and your one approval

How it works

Who does whatStage 1: Brief (`plan.md`)Stage 2: Module map (`modules.md`)Stage 3: Architecture (`architecture.md`)Stage 4: UI and UX decisions (`mockups/`)Stage 5: SequencesStage 6: Self-checkStage 7: One approvalChanging an approved planSpeaking to the operator

What the agent is told it is for: Plan a project or phase with Kompass Skills — brief, deep module map, architecture, UI/UX decisions with interactive HTML mockups, decision records and the canonical planning page, ending in one approval. Use at the start of a project or phase, or when the operator wants to plan, re-plan or review the plan.

kompass-build

91 lines

Builds one unit from start to finish and writes its hand-over.

Use when: For one unit, usually started by kompass-run.

Reads

  • Plan and module map
  • The latest sequence hand-over and your walkthrough feedback
  • The unit brief
  • Hand-overs of the units it depends on and the last two delivered
  • Its decisions and mockup

Leaves behind

  • Failing test first, then the fix in the owning module
  • Independent review on the pull request
  • Merged code once CI is green
  • The unit hand-over: what changed, tests, review findings, decisions, known issues, a note for the next unit, evidence

Stops for you

  • A locked file
  • A cause that cannot be proven
  • A change to the approved outcome
  • A destructive data change
  • An irreversible outside action

Who does what

Each model does the work it is best at. Every model runs at medium effort by default and is pushed to high effort when the work needs it: when one cause fails twice, when a builder fails twice on the same test, and for reviews of units that touch privacy, figures or access. Models are named by family, so each role moves to the newest model of its family on its own.

Coordinator

Opus · medium effort

The main session in every skill. It plans, writes units, decides each build's approach, briefs the helpers, judges what they return and writes every hand-over.

Why this model: Judgement and adversarial thinking: Opus is strongest at deciding what to build and spotting what is wrong.

kompass-builder

Sonnet · medium effort

Writes the code for one bounded piece of a unit, test first, inside its owned files.

Why this model: Coding from a precise brief: Sonnet writes good code quickly and costs far less, so it does the bulk of the typing.

Open design questions

  1. Should a builder pushed to high effort stay on Sonnet, or should a second failure at high effort move the piece to Opus?

kompass-reviewer

Opus · medium effort

Checks a unit's changes independently and approves or asks for changes, on correctness, privacy, evidence and ownership.

Why this model: Adversarial checking: a second Opus, in a fresh context, with no stake in the code it reviews.

Open design questions

  1. Which other kinds of unit, beyond privacy, figures and access, should always get a high-effort review?

kompass-searcher

Haiku · medium effort

Answers one bounded search or research question across the code, the Kompass records, git history or the web, and returns pointers with short excerpts.

Why this model: Searching and reading at volume: Haiku is fast and cheap, so wide sweeps cost little and keep the coordinator's context clean.

Open design questions

  1. Should it also do outside research (other products, library documentation), or should that stay with Opus?

What keeps it safe

Safety lives in GitHub and CI, where it holds whichever tool writes the code. Nothing else blocks on your Mac.

  • Main only takes changes through pull requests, with one required CI check.
  • Each pull request is re-tested on top of the latest main before it merges.
  • Pull requests merge automatically once green.
  • CI runs the full tests, the two tripwires (locked files; switched-off tests) and the scanners, whichever tool wrote the code.
  • The destructive-command guard on your Mac stays as a backstop.
